newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: Ariane rocket launches U.S., Argentine satellites.
newsitem.headline: Ariane rocket launches U.S., Argentine satellites.

text.p: Western Europe's 93rd Ariane rocket placed U.S. and Argentine satellites into orbit after a textbook launch late on Thursday.
The Ariane 44L rocket equipped with four liquid strap-on boosters blasted off at 7:04 p.m. (2204 GMT) with its heaviest payload, weighing more than 10,800 pounds (4.9 tonnes).
The rocket lifted off into a very cloudy equatorial night sky from the European Space Agency (ESA) launch centre on the northeast coast of South America.

Twenty minutes after takeoff space officials said the American GE-2 satellite separated from the rocket. The 5,839 lb (2.649 tonne) satellite will be used for voice, data and television broadcasting throughout North America and Hawaii. Half of the satellite's capacity will be used by direct television broadcaster PRIMESTAR.

"This (GE-2) is a revolutionary design in spacecraft technology. It has approximately 60 percent fewer parts and components than comparable satellites which makes it possible to put the same payload in space with almost 1,000 kg (2,205 lb) less weight," Walter Braun, senior vice president of California-based GE American Communications, told a pre-launch news conference.
GE American is a subsidiary of General Electric and is a successor company to RCA Communications that has operated satellites since 1973.

Braun declined to disclose the cost of GE-2. Specialists estimated the cost of the satellite, launch and insurance at more than $300 million. It was built by New Jersey-based Lockheed Martin Astro Space and is designed to operate in orbit for 15 years.

Four minutes after the release of the American satellite, NAHUEL 1A, Argentina's first satellite, was released into space. It was contracted for the Buenos Aires-based company Nahuelsat by Germany's DASA, which holds a 31 percent interest in Nahuelsat.
France's Aerospatiale built the 3,946 lb (1.79 tonne) satellite designed to provide telecommunications throughout Latin America.

"With the launch of NAHUEL, Latin America is making an enourmous step into the area of modern telecommunications ... It is an important step toward creating an efficient communications infrastructure which is absolutely essential for this strongly emerging economic area," said Werner Heinzmann, president of the Space Systems Group of DASA.
Heinzmann said the insured value of the launch and satellite was $250 million.

The combined weight of both satellites was 9,785 lb (4.44 tonnes). An additional 1,014 lb (460 kg) was used to separate the two satellites inside the rocket. It was the heaviest payload launched by an Ariane-4 since the rocket was introduced into the satellite launch market in 1988.

The Paris-based Arianespace company controls more than half the world's commercial rocket launch market. It fears, however, its lead is threatened by American consolidation -- notably the planned purchase of McDonnell Douglas Corp by Boeing.

It successfully launched 15 satellites aboard 10 Ariane-4 rockets in 1996 and signed firm contracts during the year for the launch of 19 more satellites that brings its firm launch orders to 40, worth an estimated $3.4 billion.
But on June 4, the first more powerful, new generation Ariane-5 rocket exploded 37 seconds after its maiden launch in a major setback for the European space programme.

Arianespace was scheduled to take over operations of Ariane-5 early this year -- but the new rocket's commercial future is now in doubt and a second experimental launch of the more powerful rocket is planned for July at earliest.
